value: The region's main grape in what is above all a red wine valley, grown mostly on steep terraced slopes of slate where the grapes are picked by hand.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: mainly red wines on steep slopes; vines on steep terraced cliffs of slate; Spätburgunder predominates. Ahrwein e.V.: Spätburgunder reigns, at home on the steep terraces, all grapes picked by hand. VDP: Ahr growers are Spätburgunder specialists on greywacke and slate.

value: On the Ahr's slate it gives velvety, finely structured reds whose fresh, cool climate fruit comes with an earthy edge rather than jamminess.
source_notes: Ahrwein e.V.: velvety fruity taste shaped by slate; cool nights keep acidity; cool climate gives fresh fruit aromas; finely structured. Wine Folly: definite earthiness beneath the fruit; lacks the jammy side of warm climate Pinot Noir. Deutsches Weininstitut: velvety to fiery Spätburgunder.

value: The leading white grape in a valley planted mostly with red varieties, grown on only a small part of the vineyard.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: four of five bottles are red; lively, fresh Riesling is the most common white wine produced. Ahrwein e.V.: Riesling is the front runner among Ahr whites, on a small share of the vineyard. (Falstaff adds that white wine plays only a minor role.)

value: On the Ahr it comes out racy and lively, with a crisp, piquant acidity.
source_notes: Ahrwein e.V. Riesling page: on the Ahr it tastes especially racy and piquant, sprightly and lively. Deutsches Weininstitut: lively, fresh Riesling.

value: The white specialty of the Markgräflerland in the far south of Baden near Basel, made mostly into light, fresh wines for drinking young.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: the Markgräflerland near the Swiss border cultivates the white specialty Gutedel. Badischer Wein GmbH: the Markgräflerland is planted largely with Gutedel; mostly light, fresh wines usually drunk young. Falstaff: Gutedel is the specialty of the Markgräflerland near Basel.

value: One of Baden's main white grapes and an everyday wine of the region, important around Lake Constance and often sold as Rivaner when made light and dry.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: among the main varieties; Rivaner dominates in the north; Lake Constance known above all for Pinot Noir and Müller-Thurgau. Badischer Wein GmbH: still important as an everyday wine; sold as Rivaner when light and fresh. Falstaff: Lake Constance wines mostly from Müller-Thurgau and Spätburgunder.

value: One of the Pinot family grapes that dominate Baden, suited to its warm, sunny slopes and deep limestone soils, and made mostly dry, sometimes in oak.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: the Pinot family covers most of Baden's vineyard; Weißburgunder among the main varieties. Badischer Wein GmbH: ideal conditions on sunny slopes with warm, deep, calcareous soils; usually made dry, partly in barrique.

value: One of the grapes Baden is best known for, made dry in a light, fresh style or fuller and rounder from late picked grapes or oak.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Grauburgunder among Baden's leading varieties. Badischer Wein GmbH: young, dry and fresh as a summer wine, or full bodied as Spätlese or in barrique. ProWein: voluminous, fruity Grauburgunder is what Baden stands for.

value: Baden's warmth makes it full and rounded, with ripe fruit and gentle acidity.
source_notes: Badischer Wein GmbH: low in acidity, full bodied, balanced, rich; pear, ripe apple, peach. ProWein: voluminous, fruity Grauburgunder.

value: Baden's main grape, at its best in the Kaiserstuhl, Tuniberg, Breisgau and Ortenau, made mostly dry and increasingly also as rosé or Blanc de Noirs.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: the Pinot family led by Spätburgunder; Pinot varieties prevail in Breisgau, Kaiserstuhl, Tuniberg; Pinot Noir leads in the Ortenau. VDP: Spätburgunder is the main grape. Badischer Wein GmbH: great sites in Kaiserstuhl, Tuniberg, Breisgau, Ortenau; mostly dry, increasingly rosé or Blanc de Noir. Falstaff: the most powerful Pinot wines grow on Tuniberg and Kaiserstuhl.

value: In Baden's warm south it gains body, giving fuller, more velvety and powerful reds than in Germany's cooler valleys, above all on the volcanic Kaiserstuhl.
source_notes: Badischer Wein GmbH: fruity fresh to full and velvety; reds carry the warmth and intensity of the region. Falstaff: the most powerful Pinot wines of Baden grow on Tuniberg and the Kaiserstuhl. Wine Folly: the warmer South specialises in Pinot Noir with sweet fruit.

value: One of Franken's two main white grapes beside Silvaner, softer and more approachable on the Keuper soils of the Steigerwald.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Franconia's second most planted variety, delicately aromatic, now made in a modern style. ProWein: important white variety; Steigerwald Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau softer and more accessible.

value: Franken's signature grape, grown here for centuries and at home on the shell limestone around Würzburg, its dry wines often bottled in the flat, round Bocksbeutel.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: hallmark of Franconian winemaking, thrives on shell limestone and Keuper. VDP: Silvaner, grown here for over 350 years, dominates; shell limestone in the Maindreieck around Würzburg; dry wines filled into the Bocksbeutel. Wine Folly: Franken Silvaner bottled in stubby green Bocksbeutel.

value: On the shell limestone around Würzburg it turns firm, mineral and spicy, while on the Keuper of the Steigerwald it grows broader and fuller.
source_notes: Falstaff: Silvaner has a mineral nature; shell limestone around Würzburg brings spice; on the gypsum Keuper of the Steigerwald it grows to great volume. ProWein: shell limestone gives distinct minerality and structure; Keuper gives fine spiciness and fruit.

value: One of the region's main white grapes beside Riesling and Grauburgunder, among the Pinot varieties now gaining ground here.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: main varieties Riesling, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Pinot Blanc, Silvaner. Weinbauverband Hessische Bergstraße: Grau and Weißburgunder strongly on the rise.

value: Beside Riesling the main white grape of the region, made in styles from light and fruity to full and rich.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: white varieties dominate, especially Riesling and Pinot Gris. Weinbauverband Hessische Bergstraße: Grauburgunder on the rise, fine fruity white styles. ProWein: Ruländer (Pinot Gris) important, full bodied and complex.

value: The main red grape of a region that grows mostly white wine.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: whites dominate; Pinot Noir among the main varieties. ProWein: Pinot Noir the most important red variety.

value: Here it tends to be delicate and finely built, with fine tannins.
source_notes: Weinbauverband Hessische Bergstraße: the filigree, typical Spätburgunder. ProWein: Pinot Noirs develop a beautiful fruitiness with fine tannins.

value: The flagship grape of the region, grown mainly on the slopes at the foot of the Odenwald around Bensheim and Heppenheim.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: white varieties dominate at the foot of the Odenwald, especially Riesling. Weinbauverband Hessische Bergstraße: the flagship is still Riesling; centres Auerbach, Bensheim, Heppenheim. Falstaff: Riesling dominates; wines from Heppenheim and Bensheim.

value: It is a little slimmer and firmer than Rheingau Riesling, with a fresh, hearty character.
source_notes: Falstaff: Riesling from Heppenheim and Bensheim is somewhat slimmer and firmer than that of the Rheingau. Weinbauverband Hessische Bergstraße: Bergstraße wines are of a fresh, hearty kind (said of the region's wines in general).

value: Weißburgunder
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut lists the main varieties as Riesling, Spätburgunder, Weißburgunder, Müller-Thurgau. Mittelrhein Wein e.V.: Weißburgunder vines in Koblenz.

value: A minor white grape in a valley given over mostly to Riesling, one of the Pinot varieties grown beside it.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Riesling covers almost two thirds; Weißburgunder among the main varieties. VDP: mainly Riesling, but also Pinot family varieties. ProWein: Pinot Blanc listed third after Riesling and Pinot Noir.

value: The undisputed main grape, grown on steep, often terraced slopes of slate and greywacke above the Rhine.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Riesling the undisputed star; soils mainly slate and greywacke. VDP: mainly Riesling clinging to slate; extremely steep and terraced vineyards. Mittelrhein Wein e.V.: Riesling thrives on the slate of the southern Mittelrhein.

value: On the slate of the gorge it is taut and mineral, with pronounced acidity and a more austere build than Rheingau Riesling.
source_notes: Falstaff: more austere and pithy than the Rheingau, more floral and berry like than the Mosel. ProWein: slate gives Riesling a distinct minerality; elegance, freshness and pronounced acidity. Mittelrhein Wein e.V.: mineral rich slate soils.

value: The defining grape of the Mosel, Saar and Ruwer, planted on most of the vineyard and above all on the steep slate slopes, and made in every style from dry to nobly sweet.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: growers are Riesling specialists; slate and Riesling dominate; famous noble sweet as well as dry wines. Moselwein e.V.: Riesling the most important grape, suited to the steep slate sites, made in every sweetness level. VDP: Riesling clearly dominant. Falstaff: grows almost wherever a steep slope rises on slate; dry to Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein.

value: One of the region's main white grapes beside Riesling and the Pinot varieties.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: main varieties Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc. ProWein: listed after Riesling among the leading varieties.

value: The leading grape of the region, grown on its unusual mix of slate, volcanic rock, quartzite and sandstone soils.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: dominant Riesling; vines on slate, volcanic porphyry, loess and loam. Falstaff: Riesling dominates along the upper, middle and lower Nahe; soils of slate, quartzite, Rotliegend and volcanic rock.

value: The very varied soils give it marked minerality and layered, complex aromas.
source_notes: Falstaff: slate gives Riesling minerality and complex aromas. VDP: geological variety gives the wines depth and complexity. ProWein: Nahe Rieslings known for elegance, minerality and balanced acidity.

value: One of the Pinot varieties gaining ground in the Pfalz, as important as Riesling in the south of the region below Neustadt.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris gaining significant ground; Grauburgunder among the main varieties. VDP: south of Neustadt the Pinot family plays just as important a role as Riesling, with Grauer Burgunder on shell limestone.

value: A leading red grape of the region, at its best on limestone, both in the south of the Pfalz and on the limestone sites north of Bad Dürkheim around Kallstadt and Laumersheim.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Spätburgunder among the main varieties of Germany's largest red wine region. VDP: south of Neustadt shell limestone suits grand Spätburgunder. Falstaff: on the limestone north of Bad Dürkheim, in Kallstadt and Laumersheim, Pinot Noir has great importance.

value: The region's leading grape, at its most famous in the Mittelhaardt around Forst and Deidesheim, and made mostly dry.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Riesling the undisputed number one. Falstaff: around Forst and Deidesheim almost exclusively Riesling. VDP: a breeding ground for grand dry wines.

value: In one of Germany's sunniest regions it is riper and fuller than in the northern valleys while keeping its finesse.
source_notes: VDP: cool enough for elegant, delicate wines, warm enough for power and full bodied balance; one of the warmest regions. Falstaff: Riesling here brings together refinement and fullness.

value: The region's red grape, centred on the steep slate slopes around Assmannshausen in the west of the Rheingau.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Spätburgunder particularly well known in Assmannshausen. VDP: Spätburgunder at home on the steep slate slopes of the lower Rheingau near Assmannshausen. Falstaff: Pinot Noir especially in the red wine stronghold of Assmannshausen with its slate soils.

value: The dominant grape, covering most of the vineyard along the long south facing slope between the wooded Taunus hills and the Rhine.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: highest share of Riesling of any German region; thrives on dry, stony, south facing slopes; Taunus protects. VDP: vineyards descend from the Taunus southward to the Rhine; highest proportion of Riesling. Falstaff: nearly 80 percent Riesling.

value: The leading red grape in a region that grows mostly white wine.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: the red wine boom driven particularly by Dornfelder. Rheinhessenwein e.V.: among reds Dornfelder and Spätburgunder dominate. ProWein: on the red side Dornfelder still dominates.

value: One of the region's main white grapes beside Riesling and Silvaner.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: main varieties Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder, Silvaner. Rheinhessenwein e.V.: Riesling, the white Pinot varieties, Müller-Thurgau and Silvaner shape the region.

value: The region's leading white grape, at its most distinctive on the red slate of the Roter Hang at Nierstein.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Riesling first among main varieties; red slaty Rotliegendes in the riverfront vineyards of Nackenheim and Nierstein. ProWein: Riesling's character especially multifaceted on the Roter Hang in Nierstein. VDP: founding estates on the Roter Hang between Mainz and Nierstein.

value: A traditional white grape here; Rheinhessen and Franken are the two main homes of Silvaner in Germany.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: around 43 percent of all German Silvaner grows in Rheinhessen. Wine Folly: primary regions for Silvaner are Rheinhessen and Franken. Rheinhessenwein e.V.: Silvaner among the grapes that shape the region.

value: One of the few red grapes, beside Portugieser and Spätburgunder, in a region that makes mostly white wine.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: reds a quarter of vineyards, particularly Portugieser, Dornfelder, Pinot Noir, Zweigelt. ProWein: white varieties dominate; reds such as Dornfelder, Portugieser and Pinot Noir also play a role.

value: One of the region's two main grapes beside Weißburgunder, made mostly dry.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Pinot Blanc and Müller-Thurgau among the most important varieties. Falstaff: Müller-Thurgau among the most typical wines; the dry style is characteristic of the region.

value: Low yields give it more delicacy here than usual, a light, fruity wine with moderate acidity.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: thanks to the low yield it reveals surprising delicacy. ProWein: fruity Müller-Thurgau with moderate acidity; light wines.

value: The grape the region is proudest of, grown on its shell limestone slopes and made mostly dry.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: the region takes particular pride in its Pinot Blanc. Falstaff: Pinot Blanc among the most typical wines, on mineral shell limestone; dry style characteristic. Wine Folly: Sachsen and Saale-Unstrut make remarkable Pinot Blanc.

value: The cool nights of this northern region make it fresh, fine and mineral rather than broad.
source_notes: ProWein: Pinot Blanc from the Freyburger Schweigenberg shows fine fruit, minerality and freshness. VDP: wines of Sachsen and Saale-Unstrut fresh, fragrant and filigreed. Deutsches Weininstitut: sunny days and cool nights give delicate, crisp wines.

value: One of the region's three typical white grapes, made mostly dry.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Riesling among the main varieties. Falstaff: Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Blanc and Riesling the most typical wines; dry style characteristic.

value: One of the region's main white grapes beside Riesling and Weißburgunder.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: main varieties Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir. Falstaff: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling and the white Pinot varieties lead the planting statistics.

value: One of the region's main white grapes and among the wines Saxony is best known for.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Pinot Blanc among the main varieties. Falstaff: white Pinot varieties at the top of the planting statistics. Wine Folly: Sachsen and Saale-Unstrut make remarkable Pinot Blanc.

value: One of the white Pinot varieties among the region's main grapes.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Pinot Gris among the main varieties. Falstaff: the white Pinot varieties are at the top of the planting statistics (Grauburgunder not named separately).

value: A leading grape of the Elbe valley, where this late ripening variety now ripens well on the steep slopes.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: the late ripening Riesling has become the most important grape variety. Falstaff: Riesling among the leading varieties. ProWein: steep slopes known for Riesling.

value: The swing between warm days and cool nights gives fresh, fine boned wines with intense aromas and a touch of minerality.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: alternation of daytime warmth and cool nights enhances aroma. VDP: wines fresh, fragrant, filigreed, aromatic and intense. ProWein: whites, especially Riesling, show freshness, fruit and fine minerality.

value: The region's most prized red and a Württemberg specialty, made both as a light, fruity everyday wine and as a concentrated, tannic red often aged in wood.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Württemberg more closely associated than any region with Lemberger. VDP: proud of a very special red grape, Lemberger. Echt Württemberger (cooperative wine body): light fruity versions and concentrated, tannic reds; suited to wood. Wine Folly: fast becoming Württemberg's flagship serious red.

value: Here it is spicy and peppery, with dark berry fruit and a firm yet fresh structure.
source_notes: VDP: powerful, spicy wines on calcareous soils. Wine Folly: black pepper, dark berries, earthy, juicy and fresh. Echt Württemberger: blackberry, blackcurrant, good structure, pleasant acidity.

value: One of the region's main red grapes, less demanding of site than Pinot Noir and happy on heavier loess and loam soils.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Schwarzriesling plays a significant role in red wine. Echt Württemberger: typical of Württemberg; less demanding of site than Trollinger, Lemberger or Spätburgunder; likes loess loam soils. Falstaff: Pinot Meunier among the red varieties making up most of the vineyard.

value: It makes a fruity, softer and more elegant red than Spätburgunder, with a scent of red berries and a slightly bitter finish.
source_notes: Echt Württemberger: ruby to brick red, red berry scent, elegant body, bittersweet finish. Badischer Wein GmbH (neighbouring Baden): a fruity, softer alternative to Spätburgunder.

value: An important red grape here beside Trollinger, Lemberger and Schwarzriesling, usually made as a serious wine for the table.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: Spätburgunder plays a significant role; enjoyed as a refined companion to cuisine. Falstaff: Pinot Noir among the main red varieties. Wine Folly: planted less here than in Baden.

value: It leans fresh and tart here, with sour cherry fruit and fine tannins.
source_notes: Wine Folly: tart fruit of rhubarb and sour cherry, fine tannins, freshness. ProWein: elegant Pinot Noir with a fine tannin profile in the Remstal.

value: The region's main white grape, at its best in the cooler, higher Rems valley east of Stuttgart.
source_notes: Deutsches Weininstitut: about half of all white wine is Riesling, the most important white. Falstaff: the high altitude, cool Rems Valley with its delicate Riesling. Wine Folly: look to the Remstal for Riesling.

value: In Württemberg it is light and moderate in alcohol, with lively acidity and little tannin.
source_notes: VDP: Trollinger notable for its moderate alcohol. Wine Folly: vivacious, light bodied, snappy acidity, subdued tannins.
